scope: Statements quoted verbatim from NCCIH “Usefulness and Safety” fact sheets (U.S. National Institutes of Health; public domain). Only medicines or groups that a quoted sentence names are matched. Not finding a statement does not mean a combination is safe.
general_quote: some herbs and medicines interact in harmful ways.

st-johns-wort.title: St. John's Wort: Usefulness and Safety

conditions.pregnancy: Pregnant, trying to conceive or breastfeeding
conditions.heart_bp_kidney: High blood pressure, heart or kidney condition
conditions.ragweed: Allergic to ragweed, daisies or marigolds
conditions.hormone_sensitive: Hormone-sensitive condition (e.g. breast, uterine or prostate cancer)

rules.quote: St. John’s wort can weaken the effects of many medicines, including crucially important medicines such as:

items.sjw_antidepressant: Some antidepressants, including amitriptyline and bupropion
items.cyclosporine: Cyclosporine, which prevents the body from rejecting transplanted organs
items.sjw_anticonvulsant: Some drugs used to prevent seizures, including phenytoin and carbamazepine
items.digoxin: Some heart medications, including digoxin and ivabradine
items.ivabradine: Some heart medications, including digoxin and ivabradine
items.hiv: Some HIV drugs, including indinavir and nevirapine
items.sjw_cancer: Some cancer medications, including irinotecan, imatinib, and docetaxel

rules.quote: taking St. John’s wort with certain antidepressants or other drugs that affect serotonin (a substance produced by some nerve cells) may lead to increased serotonin-related side effects, which can be serious.
St. John’s wort can interact in dangerous, sometimes life-threatening ways with a variety of medicines.
It may be unsafe to use St. John’s wort during pregnancy because it may increase the risk of birth defects.
Ginkgo may increase the risk of bleeding in people who are taking anticoagulant drugs, such as warfarin.
It might cause early labor or extra bleeding during delivery if used near that time.

For example, a study funded by the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH) found that levels of metformin—the most commonly prescribed diabetes medicine—decreased about 25 percent in healthy adults who were given goldenseal extract plus metformin. This drop was enough to potentially hinder glucose control in people with type 2 diabetes taking metformin.
Goldenseal may change the way your body processes many medications.
rules.effect: changes how many medicines are processed

rules.quote: Women who are pregnant or breastfeeding should not use goldenseal, and it should not be given to infants.
Some commercial goldenseal products have been found to contain other herbs or ingredients not listed on the label in addition to or instead of goldenseal.

herbs.name: Red yeast rice
herbs.identity_note: Not a plant: a mold (Monascus purpureus) fermented on rice.

rules.quote: Monacolin K is structurally identical to the medicine lovastatin.
rules.effect: same compound as a statin drug

rules.quote: Red yeast rice products can have the same types of drug interactions as statin drugs and therefore may interfere with certain medicines or increase the chance for side effects.
Red yeast rice products are not recommended for those who are pregnant or lactating.
Levels of monacolin K and lovastatin are not usually included on product labels.

variants.label: Deglycyrrhizinated (DGL)
variants.quote: Oral licorice products that do not contain glycyrrhizin (deglycyrrhizinated licorice) might be safe for up to 4 months.

rules.quote: Interactions between licorice and corticosteroids have been reported.

Even small amounts of glycyrrhizin from licorice root products have been linked to severe adverse effects in people who consume a lot of salt, in people with hypertension, and in people with heart or kidney conditions.

Taking garlic supplements may increase the risk of bleeding. If you take garlic supplements, make sure to tell your health care providers. This is especially important if you are going to have surgery or if you take medicines, such as anticoagulants or aspirin, that may also affect bleeding.
Taking garlic supplements may increase the risk of bleeding.
Kava should not be used together with other substances that have sedative effects, such as benzodiazepines or alcohol.
Various kava products have been linked to rare cases of liver injury, some of which have been serious or even fatal.
Green tea at high doses has been shown to reduce blood levels and, therefore, the effectiveness of the drug nadolol, a beta-blocker used for high blood pressure and heart problems.
Green tea extract can reduce blood levels of the cholesterol-lowering drug atorvastatin.
A study funded by the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health showed an interaction between green tea and the drug raloxifene, which is used to treat osteoporosis.
Although uncommon, liver injury has been reported in some people who used green tea products, primarily green tea extracts in tablet or capsule form.
If you have diabetes, consult your health care provider before using Asian ginseng.
Asian ginseng may worsen autoimmune disorders and interfere with blood clotting.
Some studies of Asian ginseng suggest it may be unsafe when taken orally during pregnancy.

variants.label: Absorption-enhanced formulation
variants.quote: Highly bioavailable formulations of curcumin, which enhance the body’s ability to absorb the curcumin, may harm your liver.

rules.quote: Many curcumin products with increased bioavailability are on the market, and liver damage has been reported in some people who have consumed these bioavailable formulations.
The use of turmeric supplements during pregnancy may be unsafe.
Because it is possible (though not proven) that valerian might have a sleep-inducing effect, it should not be taken along with alcohol or sedatives.

There is evidence that ashwagandha might interact with some medications, including those for diabetes and high blood pressure, medicines that decrease the immune system response (immunosuppressants), sedatives, anti-seizure medications (anticonvulsants), and thyroid hormone medications.
Ashwagandha is not recommended for people who are about to have surgery, or for those who have autoimmune or thyroid disorders.
Ashwagandha should be avoided during pregnancy and should not be used while breastfeeding.
Although it is rare, there have been a number of cases that link liver injury to ashwagandha supplements.

There is conflicting evidence about whether echinacea interacts with some drugs metabolized by the liver, and there are theoretical reasons to suspect that echinacea might interact with immunosuppressants or caffeine.
However, some people have allergic reactions to echinacea, which may be severe.
Cases of liver damage—some very serious—have been reported in people taking products labeled as black cohosh.
Black cohosh may not be safe for use during pregnancy or while breastfeeding.
Some commercial black cohosh products have been found to contain the wrong herb or to contain mixtures of black cohosh and other herbs that are not listed on the label.

Cases of serious medical events, including abnormal heart rhythms, heart attacks, and strokes, have been reported in people who had taken bitter orange products, but most of the products contained multiple ingredients rather than bitter orange alone.
It may not be safe to use bitter orange during pregnancy or while breastfeeding, and data from animal experiments suggest that substances in bitter orange might decrease milk production.

Of 23 products with labels that stated the amount of synephrine in the product, only 5 contained amounts of synephrine close to that indicated on the label (between 80 and 120 percent of the stated amount).
Do not use yohimbe if you are taking types of antidepressant medications called monoamine oxidase inhibitors or tricyclic antidepressants.
Yohimbine, a component of yohimbe, has been associated with cardiac arrhythmia (irregular heartbeat), blood pressure problems, heart attacks, and seizures.
It might be unsafe to use yohimbe orally (taken by mouth) during pregnancy or while breastfeeding.
Milk thistle may cause allergic reactions, particularly among people who are allergic to related plants (for example, ragweed, chrysanthemum, marigold, and daisy).

Some products have been found to contain amounts of silymarin substantially different from what’s stated on the label or to be contaminated with pesticides, microorganisms, or mycotoxins (harmful substances produced by molds or other fungi).

Interactions between chamomile and some drugs metabolized by the liver and warfarin (a blood thinner) have been reported, and there are theoretical reasons to suspect that chamomile might interact with other drugs as well, such as sedatives.
Preliminary studies suggest that taking chamomile along with birth control pills might decrease the effects of birth control pills.

Interactions between chamomile and some drugs metabolized by the liver and warfarin (a blood thinner) have been reported, and there are theoretical reasons to suspect that chamomile might interact with other drugs as well, such as sedatives.
People are more likely to experience allergic reactions to chamomile if they’re allergic to related plants such as ragweed, chrysanthemums, marigolds, or daisies.
In addition, chamomile might worsen any condition that is sensitive to exposure to estrogen, such as breast or uterine cancer.

variants.label: Labeled “tejocote root”
variants.quote: In January 2024, the FDA published a list of products, including dietary supplements labeled “tejocote root” (C. mexicana), that actually contain yellow oleander, a toxic plant known to cause harm to the nervous system, heart, stomach, and intestines.

rules.quote: It’s unclear why, but one possibility is that hawthorn might have interacted with drugs the patients were taking.
Large doses may cause a harmful drop in blood sugar.
Fenugreek is not safe for use during pregnancy in amounts greater than those found in food; its use has been linked to increased risks of birth defects in both animals and people.
There is conflicting evidence about whether cranberry interacts with the anticoagulant (blood thinner) warfarin.
Passionflower might interact with some anesthesia drugs, so avoid its use before surgery unless recommended by a health care provider.
Passionflower should not be used during pregnancy as it may induce uterine contractions and possibly lead to other problems.
Capsules containing peppermint oil are often enteric-coated to reduce the likelihood of heartburn.
Saw palmetto may be unsafe for use during pregnancy or while breastfeeding.

ambiguous.source_quote: Asian ginseng is one of several types of ginseng.
There are two types of chamomile: German chamomile and Roman chamomile.
Blue cohosh may cause adverse effects such as high blood pressure, high blood sugar, and chest pain.

ai_medicine_groups.note: AI understanding of how a person describes a medicine. Used only above the threshold; otherwise the medicine stays unrecognised. Evaluation: reports/ai_medicine_understanding_v2_2026-11-12.json

groups.label: a blood thinner (anticoagulant)
groups.description: A blood thinner (anticoagulant) such as warfarin, Coumadin, Eliquis or Xarelto, taken to prevent blood clots and stroke.
prototypes: Blood thinning medicine to prevent blood clots.

groups.label: daily aspirin
groups.description: Daily low-dose aspirin, a baby aspirin taken for the heart.
prototypes: Aspirin taken daily in a low dose for the heart.

groups.label: birth control pills
groups.description: Birth control pills, oral contraceptives taken to prevent pregnancy.

groups.label: an antidepressant
groups.description: An antidepressant for depression or anxiety, such as an SSRI like Zoloft, Prozac or Lexapro.
prototypes: Antidepressant medicine prescribed for depression and anxiety.

groups.label: a sleeping pill or sedative
groups.description: A sleeping pill or sedative for insomnia, such as Ambien, or a benzodiazepine like Xanax or Valium.

groups.label: an anti-seizure medicine
groups.description: An anti-seizure medicine for epilepsy, such as Keppra, Dilantin or Lamictal.
prototypes: Anticonvulsant medicine to prevent seizures and epileptic fits.

groups.label: a statin (cholesterol medicine)
groups.description: A statin to lower cholesterol, such as Lipitor, Crestor or Zocor.
prototypes: Cholesterol lowering medicine, a statin tablet.

groups.label: a diabetes medicine
groups.description: A diabetes medicine to lower blood sugar, such as metformin, insulin or Ozempic.
prototypes: Medicine for diabetes to control blood sugar.

groups.label: a blood-pressure medicine
groups.description: A blood pressure medicine for hypertension, such as lisinopril, amlodipine, losartan, a beta blocker or a water pill (diuretic).
prototypes: A water pill, a diuretic medicine that helps remove excess fluid.
Medicine to lower high blood pressure and treat hypertension.

groups.label: a steroid (corticosteroid)
groups.description: A steroid pill such as prednisone, taken for inflammation, asthma flare-ups or arthritis.

groups.label: a thyroid hormone medicine
groups.description: Thyroid hormone pills, such as levothyroxine or Synthroid, for an underactive thyroid.
prototypes: Thyroid hormone replacement for an underactive thyroid.

groups.label: an anti-rejection medicine (immunosuppressant)
groups.description: An anti-rejection medicine after an organ transplant, an immunosuppressant such as tacrolimus or cyclosporine.
prototypes: Immunosuppressant medicine to prevent rejection after organ transplant.
